text: DR planning discipline doesn't change platform to platform: define RPO and RTO, build a backup strategy that meets them, test the restore, document the runbook. What changes on MySQL is which real tools you're assembling into that plan.

Recovery Point Objective, how much data loss is acceptable, and Recovery Time Objective, how long recovery can take, should drive tool choice rather than the other way around. That's the same starting question a SQL Server DBA asks before picking a backup strategy.

A small database with a loose RPO can run on nightly mysqldump plus binlog retention. A large, high-write database needs weekly full XtraBackup with daily incrementals, still backed by continuous binary logging for point-in-time precision when restoring.

An untested backup isn't a real backup, and that applies with zero modification to MySQL. A genuine test means actually restoring to a separate environment, verifying the data, and timing the whole process against your RTO before an outage forces you to find out.

That measure-first discipline extends beyond backups into every other area of running MySQL well. Chapter Ten starts with MySQL performance tuning methodology — the same measure, identify, change, verify loop, applied through MySQL's own tools.
